articles.title: Analysis-Israel's election may change its leader, but not Iran war policy
articles.summary: By Samia NakhoulDUBAI, Oct 21 (Reuters) - Israel's election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say.That is because the strategic assumptions underpinning Israeli policy were hardened by the October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israeli communities by Palestinian militant group Hamas andby the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis deny launching drones towards Saudi Arabia's Medina

articles.title: Turkey plans mandate to send military personnel to Saudi Arabia, ruling party official says

articles.title: World falling 'dangerously short' on climate action: UN chief
articles.summary: Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6C warming this century, the UN warned Wednesday. articles.title: Israel becomes Pacific Islands Forum partner
articles.summary: Israel has joined the inter-governmental Pacific Islands Forum as a partner offering climate change adaptation and water management expertise, its foreign ministry said Wednesday. articles.title: Iran says Saudi Arabia, Houthis have not answered mediation offer

articles.title: Eastern Libya parliament approves maritime deal with Turkey, drawing Greek rejection

articles.title: Explainer-What's at stake for Trump in Israel's deadlocked election?

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc secured the most seats in Israel's parliament but still lost its parliamentary majority on Tuesday despite Trump having endorsed him against a rival alliance of parties led by hawkish former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

With the turnout in Tuesday's election at a record high and nearly 86% of votes tallied, Israel's three main broadcasters put Netanyahu's bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties on course to win 53 seats in parliament, with the opposition bloc of rival Gadi Eisenkot trailing on 48.

He threatens, he warns, he issues ultimatums, and then he expects the world to believe that he has everything under control. But there comes a point when even the loudest threats begin to lose their effect. Iran may well be that point for Trump. He seems to have underestimated a country whose political instincts, historical memory and civilisational confidence cannot be understood through the narrow lens of American power.
